newsitem.title: UK: Right-wing economists attack UK govt jobs scheme.
newsitem.headline: Right-wing economists attack UK govt jobs scheme.

text.p: The British government's welfare-to-work programme was heavily criticised by some of the country's leading right-wing economists on Thursday who said it offered nothing new.

Patrick Minford, economics professor at Cardiff University and former independent adviser to the Treasury, attacked the scheme which aims to offer all 18-24 year-olds work experience to help them enter the job-market.
He told a seminar at the free-market think-tank The Adam Smith Institute that welfare-to-work was tinkering with a benefit system that offered no room for further fine-tuning.
Minford, formerly economics professor at Liverpool University, said unemployment benefit should be withdrawn altogether, and the young be told it is up to them to carve out a future for themselves.
"We should move towards a system of self-provision and get away from the benefit system," Minford said.
"I would abolish the benefit system for all new claimants, and tell all those entering the labour market they must have an Asian-style "fortune" account."
Most parts of Asia do not offer a welfare system, instead encouraging those in work to save in a personal savings account.
Labour plans to spend around 3.5 billion pounds ($5.9 billion) raised from its one-off windfall tax on privatised utilities to create posts for 250,000 young and long-term unemployed people.

Roderick Nye, economist at the Social Market Foundation, said the running of the scheme should be transferred wholesale to the private sector. Then employers would be more likely to show confidence in it.
"The government could easily have funded the scheme by transferring its running to the private sector."
Nye said similar private-run schemes in the United States were more effective than governmental employment schemes in finding jobs for the unemployed.
"Privatisation of the scheme is my benchmark to judge whether or not Labour is taking welfare-to-work seriously," he said.

Alan Howarth, Minister for education and employment, put the case for the government at the seminar and said the purpose of welfare-to-work was to enhance the employability of those joining the scheme.

But while many employers were putting themselves forward to offer jobs, which the government will subsidise by between 60-75 pounds per week, welfare-to-work would not create new jobs in the economy, he said.
"Schemes to get to work won't in themselves generate additional jobs. Only sustained economic growth will create new jobs."

Minford saw unemployment levels falling from current levels around 5.7 percent to around 2.5 percent over the next three years, as Britain's economic recovery reabsorbed many unemployed people back into work.
